top.headline: Trump Offers Dana White the White House Press Secretary Job
top.blurb: Trump announced on Truth Social that UFC CEO Dana White has been offered the press secretary job, calling him "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and asking him to bring fighters Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov along to counter "the Lunatic Left." White has no government experience and hasn't said whether he'll accept; he would be Trump's seventh press secretary since January.

top.headline: Texas Democrats Flip the State House, Put Abbott's Voucher Program on Death Row
top.blurb: Democrats won the Texas House for the first time in 24 years, and governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is vowing to unwind Greg Abbott's roughly $1 billion school voucher program, though Republicans held the Senate. At least 13 Republicans Abbott campaigned for lost or are trailing, and one state representative predicts the voucher program will be "unrecognizable, if not extinct" within a term.

top.headline: A Judge Halts Trump's Triumphal Arch — and Congress Says It Can Kill It for Good
top.blurb: A federal judge paused construction for 14 days on Trump's planned 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery, just after a Trump-aligned commission approved it 8-4. Democrats, newly in control of Congress after the midterms, say budget language can block it even though it's privately funded — a test of how far Congress can check a president's pet building projects.

top.headline: Karnataka Election Office Admits Duplicate Voter IDs Were Generated for Hundreds During SIR
top.blurb: Karnataka's chief electoral office admitted multiple voter IDs were generated for the same people during the special intensive revision of rolls, after The Hindu found 803 IDs linked to 397 people in Mahadevapura. Officials blamed duplicate applications and pending deletions; over 99.3 lakh names were already struck from the state's final roll.

top.headline: Ten Years After Demonetisation, the Numbers Say It Failed on Its Own Terms
top.blurb: A decade on from the 2016 note ban, more than 99% of withdrawn cash came back to banks, the currency-to-GDP ratio sits roughly where it started, and UPI's volume growth hasn't translated into proportional value, a bylined analysis argues. The piece concludes demonetisation delivered neither its stated anti-black-money goal nor lasting accountability for the disruption it caused.

top.headline: Israel's President Picks Eisenkot Over Netanyahu to Form the Next Government
top.blurb: President Isaac Herzog gave former army chief Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form Israel's next government, after 67 lawmakers recommended him against 46 for Netanyahu. Eisenkot has 28 days to build a coalition and has ruled out working with Arab-led parties, leaving the ultra-Orthodox blocs as his likeliest path to a majority.

top.headline: US Launches Task Force to Choke Off Iran's Overland Weapons Routes
top.blurb: CENTCOM has stood up Task Force Iron Gate to block Iran from moving weapons and sanctioned materials across its land borders and the Caspian Sea, extending a months-long naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz. The move comes as Iranian state media reported fresh explosions on Qeshm Island and two tankers were reportedly struck by mines in the strait.

top.headline: More Than 140,000 Rally Across France as Cost-of-Living Protests Enter a Fourth Weekend
top.blurb: France saw its fourth straight weekend of protests over the cost of living and fuel prices, with roughly 146,000 people turning out nationwide (unions say 250,000) as police deployed tear gas in Paris and Lyon. The movement began in September over conditions at French high schools before widening into a broader economic revolt.

top.headline: India Edge New Zealand by Four Runs on DLS to Take a 2-0 Series Lead in Wellington
top.blurb: India beat New Zealand by four runs on DLS in a rain-shortened second ODI at Wellington, with Gurnoor Brar's career-best 4/30 restricting the hosts to 134. Rohit Sharma, Shreyas Iyer and Axar Patel steadied a shaky chase as India took a 2-0 lead in the five-match series.

top.headline: John Malkovich Gallops Away With 'Wild Horse Nine'
top.blurb: NPR critic Bob Mondello reviews Martin McDonagh's dark comedy "Wild Horse Nine," in which John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play American operatives in 1973 Chile whose sharp banter masks something darker. Mondello calls Malkovich "a creep for the ages" and finds the film's mix of comedy and quiet grief lands, even if Rockwell gets less to do.

top.headline: Jordan Firstman on Playing a 'Club Kid' Who Discovers Fatherhood
top.blurb: In an NPR interview, Jordan Firstman discusses his directorial debut "Club Kid," a coming-of-age story about a 30-something gay party promoter who learns he has a 10-year-old son. Firstman says he drew on his own nightlife years and cast real club kids as background extras to keep the party scenes honest.

bengal.headline: Suvendu Adhikari Backs ABVP 'Clean-Up' Drive at Presidency and Jadavpur, Calls Protesters 'Cockroaches'
bengal.blurb: At a Kali Puja event, Suvendu Adhikari urged ABVP to continue its campus "clean-up" at Presidency and Jadavpur, branding student groups "cockroaches" over "Kashmir azaadi" slogans while invoking Syama Prasad Mookerjee.

bengal.headline: Bengal Makes Bengali Mandatory on Government Project Signboards
bengal.blurb: The state government ordered Bengali text on all government project information boards by November 30 after many showed only English, while also raising departmental project-approval limits from Rs 3 crore to Rs 6 crore.

travel.headline: As Loggerhead Turtles Spread West, Mediterranean Resorts Learn to Share the Sand
travel.blurb: Warming seas are pushing loggerhead turtles to nest farther west and north in the Mediterranean, and resorts in Spain, Italy and France are redesigning beach operations to coexist with them.

happy.headline: George Washington's Lost Pistol — a Gift From the Mentor He'd Later Fight Against — Surfaces at the Smithsonian
happy.blurb: British general Edward Braddock gave young Washington an ornate pistol before dying in battle; Washington treasured it through years of campaigns against the crown Braddock served, then mislaid it — and it has now resurfaced at the Smithsonian.

tech_top.headline: Data Centers Become a Political Flashpoint After Democrats' Midterm Sweep
tech_top.blurb: Voters rejected data centers in dozens of local ballot measures, and candidates who ran against them won even where the projects weren't on the ballot — including Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who unseated Greg Abbott. Water use and secretive permitting fueled the backlash, and tighter rules now look likely to reach even Elon Musk's projects.
tech_top.pm_note: If your roadmap assumes limitless cheap compute, start modeling permitting and community-opposition risk now — a blocked data center is as real a constraint as a chip shortage.

tech_top.headline: A US Intelligence Memo Alleges China Recruited an Executive to Spy on Nvidia's CEO
tech_top.blurb: A memo based on US intelligence claims China's Ministry of State Security recruited a Megaspeed executive to gather information from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang; Nvidia called the contact "not unusual" and said it shares no classified data. It lands alongside a separate finding that a Commerce-approved buyer of advanced Nvidia chips operates out of an empty office.
tech_top.pm_note: Export-control compliance is no longer paperwork — if your supply chain touches advanced chips, assume regulators are scrutinizing your customer list as closely as your product.

tech_top.headline: Binance's CFO Departs, a Week After a $6.3 Billion Hack
tech_top.blurb: Binance CFO Kaiser Ng is leaving for a "new venture" after five years; the exchange says the move was planned months ago and isn't tied to the $6.3 billion theft that Binance and the FBI attribute to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Binance has pledged to cover the losses itself rather than pass them to users.
tech_top.pm_note: A company that can absorb a $6.3B loss without passing it to users is buying trust with its balance sheet — watch whether smaller competitors survive the same attack.

tech_101.text: Industry's new name for a data center — same water- and power-hungry multi-building site, rebranded to sound like a tech campus now that voters are rejecting data centers by that name.
A hacking group US investigators tie to North Korea, specialized in draining crypto exchanges' hot wallets — the suspected culprit behind Binance's $6.3 billion loss this month.

science.headline: After 60 Years, Chemists Finally Capture an Elusive Boron-Oxygen Molecule
science.blurb: University of Würzburg researchers, led by Holger Braunschweig, accidentally isolated stable oxoboranes — molecules with a boron-oxygen triple bond chemists had chased for over 60 years — while testing an unrelated boron compound against common ketones. The simple reaction, published in Nature Chemistry, could open a route to other long-sought molecules.

science.headline: Vera Rubin Observatory Finds Two Hidden Companions of the Milky Way — With Hundreds More Likely Out There
science.blurb: In preview data covering just 7% of the sky, Chile's Vera C. Rubin Observatory has already spotted two previously unknown Milky Way satellites: Aquarius IV, an ultra-faint galaxy 355,000 light-years out, and Rubin-GC1, a star cluster hidden behind cosmic dust. Astronomers expect the observatory's decade-long survey to turn up hundreds more, reshaping what's known about galaxy formation and dark matter.

science.headline: Earth's Polar Vortex Is Breaking Down Weeks Earlier Than Ever Recorded
science.blurb: Forecasters at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts say the Arctic stratospheric polar vortex is weakening in early November — the earliest such disruption on record, with only three comparable November events since 1958. Rossby waves surging into the stratosphere triggered the collapse, raising the odds of cold outbreaks across the Northern Hemisphere this winter.

philosophy.headline: Why the Line Between Religious Belief and Factual Belief Justifies Separating Church and State
philosophy.blurb: Religious credence is chosen and insulated from evidence, while factual belief is involuntary and drives action everywhere else — philosopher Neil Van Leeuwen and collaborators argue this psychological split, not mere tradition, is why liberal democracies bar state religion while still protecting free worship. Policies built on religious conviction can't be tested through public reasoning the way factual claims can.

philosophy.headline: Why Living With Housemates, Not Family, Finally Punctured One Writer's Self-Deceptions
philosophy.blurb: Sharing a London house with unrelated strangers forced essayist Elizabeth Oldfield to confront self-deceptions that family and solitude let her avoid, drawing on Charles Taylor's "buffered self" and Iris Murdoch's idea of seeing past one's own fantasies. Such communities only last, she argues, when built around a purpose bigger than companionship itself.

philosophy_101.text: Philosophers distinguish 'credence' — a stance you can choose to hold in one context (like a pew) and drop in another — from 'belief', which tracks evidence and follows you everywhere, including into a voting booth. The difference explains why you can respect someone's faith and still insist public policy answer to facts.
